# Question 1 — Summation Notation

**Review**

- [Week 01 §11 — Fundamental Mathematics](../study-guides/week01-basic-concepts.qmd#fundamental-mathematics)
- [Week 01 §12 — Summation Notation](../study-guides/week01-basic-concepts.qmd#summation-notation)
- [Week 01 §13 — Worked Summation Example](../study-guides/week01-basic-concepts.qmd#worked-summation-example)
- [Week 02 §1 — Review: Summation Notation](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#review-summation-notation)

**Method**

1. Translate each expression into words before calculating.
2. Identify exactly what is inside the summation sign.
3. Follow BEDMAS/PEDMAS.
4. Keep (x_i) and (y_i) paired by their common index.
5. Distinguish ((\sum X)^2) from (\sum X^2): one sums first and then squares; the other squares each observation first and then sums.
6. For (\sum(x_i-y_i)) or (\sum(x_iy_i)), work row by row before adding.
7. For ((\sum x_i)(\sum y_i)), calculate the two sums separately and multiply only at the end.
8. A constant inside a summation is applied once for every included observation.

# Question 2 — Adding a Constant to Every Score

**Review**

- [Week 03 §15 — How the Mean Changes](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#how-the-mean-changes)
- [Week 03 §33 — What Happens When Scores Are Transformed?](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#what-happens-when-scores-are-transformed)

Represent the transformation as (Y_i=X_i+c). Consider the mean and standard deviation separately.

For the mean, ask what adding the same constant to every observation does to the average.

For the standard deviation, compare the deviation (X_i-M_X) with ((X_i+c)-(M_X+c)). Use that comparison to explain what happens to the spread.

# Question 3 — Research Design and Causation

**Review**

- [Week 01 §9 — Three Basic Research Designs](../study-guides/week01-basic-concepts.qmd#three-basic-research-designs)
- [Week 01 §21 — Tutorial Preparation](../study-guides/week01-basic-concepts.qmd#tutorial-preparation)

Compare experimental, quasi-experimental, and correlational designs by asking whether there is manipulation, random assignment, and a comparison/control condition. Identify what distinguishes a true experiment, then explain how those design features reduce competing explanations. Do not stop at saying that experiments allow causal conclusions; explain why.

# Questions 4–6 — Scales of Measurement

**Review**

- [Week 02 §4 — The Four Scales of Measurement](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#the-four-scales-of-measurement)
- [Week 02 §5 — Nominal Variables](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#nominal-variables)
- [Week 02 §6 — Ordinal Variables](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#ordinal-variables)
- [Week 02 §7 — Interval Variables](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#interval-variables)
- [Week 02 §32 — Important Terms](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#important-terms)

For each variable, ask:

1. Are the values only labels or categories?
2. Can the categories be meaningfully ordered?
3. Are equal numerical differences meaningful?
4. Does zero represent a genuine absence of the measured quantity?

For **Question 4**, apply these criteria separately to every variable and justify the classification from the properties of the measurement.

For **Question 5**, classify reaction time and handedness independently.

For **Question 6**, classify the variable **as it was recorded**: the survey records ordered income ranges, not exact income values.

# Question 7 — Distribution Shape

**Review**

- [Week 02 §12 — Ungrouped Frequency Distributions](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#ungrouped-frequency-distributions)
- [Week 02 §23 — Frequency Polygons](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#frequency-polygons)

Identify where most observations are concentrated and where the few extreme observations occur. The direction of the long tail determines the direction of skew. Your sketch should show the variable on the horizontal axis and frequency on the vertical axis.

# Question 8 — Movie Ratings

## 8a — Measurement scales

Review [Week 02 §4 — The Four Scales of Measurement](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#the-four-scales-of-measurement).

Classify **film rating** and **year** separately. Ask whether each variable conveys category, order, equal intervals, and/or a meaningful zero.

## 8b — Total frequencies

**Review**

- [Week 02 §12 — Ungrouped Frequency Distributions](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#ungrouped-frequency-distributions)
- [Week 02 §13 — Frequency, Proportion, Percentage, and Cumulative Values](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#frequency-proportion-percentage-and-cumulative-values)

Sum each rating column across all years, then add the four rating totals to obtain the overall (n). Check the result by confirming that summing the yearly totals gives the same grand total.

## 8c — Percentages

Review [Week 02 §13](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#frequency-proportion-percentage-and-cumulative-values).

For each rating, calculate

[
p=\frac{f}{n}
]

and then

[
\%=p\times100.
]

The four percentages should total approximately (100%), allowing for rounding.

## 8d — Visualization

**Review**

- Week 02 sections on bar charts, histograms, and frequency polygons
- [Week 02 §35 — Practice Questions](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#practice-questions), especially **Graph Choice**

First identify whether film rating is categorical or continuous, then choose the graph appropriate to that variable type. Put rating categories on the horizontal axis and film counts on the vertical axis. Label both axes.

## 8e — Describe the graph

Review [Week 02 §25 — Graphs Can Clarify—and Mislead](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#graphs-can-clarifyand-mislead).

Describe the relative heights of the categories. Because the display is categorical, do not automatically apply continuous-distribution terms such as positive or negative skew.

## 8f — Most popular rating

**Review**

- [Week 02 §29 — The Mode](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#the-mode)
- [Week 03 §2 — The Mode](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#the-mode)

Compare the four totals from 8b. The category with the largest frequency is the modal category. Report the category and its count.

## 8g — Evaluate the claim

Use the frequency and percentage ideas in [Week 02 §13](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#frequency-proportion-percentage-and-cumulative-values) together with the mode.

Translate the citizen's statement into something the table can test. Compare the relevant count and percentage with the other categories and the total. Base the conclusion only on the supplied fictional data.

# Question 9 — Distracted vs. Not-Distracted Groups

Keep the two groups separate throughout the calculations.

## 9a — Mean

**Review**

- [Week 02 §27 — The Mean](../study-guides/week02-data-types-visualization.qmd#the-mean)
- [Week 03 §1 — Why Do We Need Measures of Center?](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#why-do-we-need-measures-of-center)

For each group, calculate

[
M=\frac{\sum X}{n}.
]

Show the sum and (n), then divide.

## 9b — Range

Review [Week 03 §22 — The Range](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#the-range).

For each group:

[
\text{Range}=X_{\max}-X_{\min}.
]

## 9c — Standard deviation

**Review**

- [Week 03 §24 — From Deviation to Variance](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#from-deviation-to-variance)
- [Week 03 §39 — Important Terms](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#important-terms)
- [Week 03 §42 — Practice Questions](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#practice-questions)

For each group:

1. Calculate the mean.
2. Calculate each deviation (X_i-M).
3. Square the deviations.
4. Sum the squared deviations to obtain (SS).
5. Apply the sample or population variance formula required by the course.
6. Take the square root of the variance.

Check the Week 3 distinction between (N) and (n-1).

## 9d — Median and mode

**Review**

- [Week 03 §2 — The Mode](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#the-mode)
- [Week 03 §3 — The Median](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#the-median)
- [Week 03 §4 — Median With an Even Number of Scores](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#median-with-an-even-number-of-scores)

Sort each group first. For the median, locate the middle position and apply the appropriate odd/even-(n) procedure. For the mode, count frequencies and check whether the group is unimodal, bimodal, multimodal, or nonmodal.

## 9e — 75th percentile

**Review**

- [Week 03 §5 — The Course's Interpolated Median Formula](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#the-courses-interpolated-median-formula)
- [Week 03 §23 — Interquartile Range](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#interquartile-range)

Use the **course's percentile procedure** rather than substituting a different software convention. Order the data, use cumulative frequency to locate the 75th percentile, and apply the course interpolation procedure when required. The 75th percentile is (Q_3).

## 9f — Compare the groups

**Review**

- [Week 03 §36 — What Should Be Reported Together?](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#what-should-be-reported-together)
- [Week 03 §38 — How the Concepts Fit Together](../study-guides/week03-central-tendency-variability.qmd#how-the-concepts-fit-together)

This is an interpretation question. Compare the groups using the descriptive statistics already calculated: mean, median, mode where informative, range, standard deviation, 75th percentile, and any obvious distributional differences.

Then decide whether those descriptive summaries are consistent with the stated prediction. Do **not** describe the difference as statistically significant unless an inferential test has actually been conducted.

# Final Self-Check

Before submitting, verify that you have:

- shown enough work for the calculations to be followed;
- kept paired (x_i) and (y_i) values aligned in Question 1;
- distinguished ((\sum X)^2) from (\sum X^2);
- justified measurement scales from their properties;
- labeled graphs clearly;
- used the course's percentile convention;
- distinguished sample from population variance where required;
- interpreted Question 9 using both center and spread.
